text:
🇺🇦 The New York Times obtained more than 700 pages of confidential Ukrainian military audits. What they show is deeply troubling.
Auditors found that Ukraine lost roughly $1.2 billion in 2024 alone to fraud, waste and mismanagement in weapons procurement.

The problems were not isolated. Ukraine repeatedly bought weapons through intermediaries at higher prices even when manufacturers offered cheaper direct deals.

Of the Defense Ministry's ten largest contractors, seven received new contracts despite previously defaulting or having senior management under criminal investigation.

Officials signed deals with 18 companies that had already failed to fulfill previous contracts. Six had never successfully completed a single contract.

One company failed to deliver any of 600 specialized drones it had promised, and was then awarded another contract for 1,950 more. It delivered only 50 on time.

In another case, Ukraine contracted for Turkish aviation rockets despite the manufacturer warning that it could not supply the promised quantities. The weapons were purchased without proof they had been properly tested.

One rocket later exploded inside a launcher and severely damaged a Ukrainian Mi-8 helicopter during a combat mission.

There is an uncomfortable strategic dimension to all of this. Ukraine is fighting a much larger country while constantly arguing that every shell, interceptor and dollar matters. If procurement corruption and mismanagement reduce how much ammunition reaches the front, the cost is measured not only in money, but it is measured in military capacity.

As one former Defense Procurement Agency adviser told the NYT: “As a result, we don’t have money to order more weapons. And we don’t have the quantity of ammunition we need.”

For a country fighting a war of attrition, that may be the most consequential finding in the entire audit.

text:
Chris Bledsoe: “When the red star of Regulus aligns just before dawn in the gaze of the Sphinx, a new knowledge shall come into the world.”

The date of the alignment is 7th October 2026.

That is the prophecy he says the Lady gave him. Not a date. A sky condition. A blue star appearing red on the eastern horizon, sitting in the line of sight of the Great Sphinx before sunrise. At that moment, he was told, humanity’s knowledge would change.

Bledsoe has repeated the wording across interviews for years. “She called it a red star. When you look at it, it looks blue. But she said when Regulus is red on the horizon, in front of the gaze of the Sphinx, before daylight… that moment would mark a change in humanity’s knowledge.” He added that the Lady framed it as an unveiling: “the darkness would be exposed and the truth would be revealed.”

She did not hand him a calendar. Later, astrologers and researchers ran the geometry and offered dates, first Easter 2026, then later windows in late summer and autumn 2026 as people rechecked heliacal rising at Giza. Bledsoe has said the Lady’s appearances to him often clustered around Easter, which is why that season stuck in the public telling. The original message stayed astronomical: Regulus, the horizon, the Sphinx’s gaze, before dawn.

What the “new knowledge” could be is the part that matters. Bledsoe has been careful not to turn it into doomsday. He has said it is not automatically the return of Jesus, though he has also said Christ consciousness is possible. In his telling it is a shift in what we are allowed to know about ourselves. Possible contents that keep surfacing in his account:

Hidden history at Giza. He links the alignment to records under or around the Sphinx, the old Hall of Records idea, material that would rewrite origins, earlier civilizations, and how long human memory actually is.

A change in the sky of power. He has said there is “a power shift in heaven that is written in the stars,” that the coming age restores the divine feminine, “the mother,” and that peace on the planet follows that restoration. The Lady, in his description, is not one culture’s goddess. He has connected her to Mary, Sophia, Isis, Hathor, Diana, Demeter, Hera. Same presence, many names.

Practical knowledge that collapses old systems. Asked what the new knowledge might look like on the ground, he has pointed at energy and propulsion. “Imagine a world without oil. Imagine a world without rockets. That kind of knowledge alone would change everything.”

Consciousness itself. The Lady told him mankind must awaken. Humanity, she showed him, had “lost its direction. It has no head or no tail.” The new knowledge, in that frame, is not only data. It is a different way of being: less captured by fear, more able to see non-physical reality, less owned by the old story.

Impact, if even part of that lands, is civilizational. Origin stories break. Energy economics break. Religious monopoly over the sacred feminine breaks. Disclosure stops being a press conference and becomes a lived change in what people treat as real. That is why the prophecy spread. It is specific enough to check against the sky and large enough to rearrange meaning if the sky ever matches the words.

Bledsoe’s line remains the cleanest version of it: when Regulus sits red on the horizon in the Sphinx’s gaze before daylight, a new knowledge is born unto humanity. The photograph of the Lady and the Sphinx is the image of that claim. The rest is whether the knowledge, when it comes, is history, physics, spirit, or all three at once.

text:
Otto von Bismarck examines US backchannel 'diplomacy' in Moscow:

Rain tapped against the tall windows of the Friedrichsruh estate. Prince Otto von Bismarck sat behind a massive oak desk covered with maps of Eastern Europe and printed intelligence dispatches dated early September 2026. Across from him, Dr Helen Vance, a senior strategic analyst, adjusted a stack of cables detailing diplomatic movements between Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv.

Bismarck picked up a summary sheet, holding it close to his eyes. He pointed a thick finger at three names printed near the top: Jared Kushner, Steve Witkoff, and John Ratcliffe.

"Explain this delegation to me again," Bismarck said, his voice deep and raspy. "Washington sends a real estate developer and a son in law to the Kremlin to negotiate the end of a major European war. Eleven days prior, the director of their central intelligence agency arrives in secret to 'deliver warnings'. Is this a coherent state strategy or an act of theatrical desperation?"

Helen leaned forward. "President Donald Trump favours personal representatives over career foreign service officers. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are his trusted envoys. They arrived in Moscow on Saturday, 5 September 2026, meeting Vladimir Putin for three hours inside the Kremlin. They brought what Washington calls a 'concrete peace proposal'. They plan to travel directly to Kyiv next to present the same framework to Volodymyr Zelensky."

Bismarck leaned back in his heavy leather chair, resting his hands on his stomach. "Back channel diplomacy is the standard currency of serious statecraft. Public diplomacy is mostly noise for domestic assemblies. When I negotiated with Saint Petersburg in 1887, we kept the Reinsurance Treaty hidden from the public and from our own allies in Vienna. But a back channel is merely a pipe. What matters is the pressure inside it. What leverage does Washington actually push through this pipe?"

"Very little to nothing right now," Helen replied. "That is the core problem. The US is simultaneously involved in a damaging military conflict with Iran. That war consumes American attention, naval assets, and air defence munitions. Ukraine faces severe shortages of Patriot missile interceptors because Washington has prioritised its own operational needs in the Middle East. Russia knows this. Russian forces have intensified their long range drone and missile attacks across Ukraine, exploiting those exact defensive gaps."

Bismarck nodded slowly, his gaze drifting to a map of the Black Sea coast. "So Washington sends envoys because its position is weakening, not because its position is strong. That is the first fundamental error. A state that seeks an emergency exit because its attention is divided elsewhere does not negotiate from strength. It begs for terms."

"CIA Director John Ratcliffe tried to counter that perception during his visit to Moscow late last month," Helen noted. "He warned Russian intelligence officials that escalating the conflict would backfire and that Russia's long term position would deteriorate. But the Kremlin largely ignored the warning. Within days, Russian strikes against Ukrainian infrastructure actually increased."

"Of course they increased," Bismarck said, a faint smile touching his moustache. "A warning unsupported by visible military force or a clear willingness to endure friction is not a deterrent. It's merely advice. When you tell an adversary that his position will deteriorate in the future, but he sees you running low on ammunition today, he calculates that your patience will break long before his reserves do. Words don't alter the balance of power. Only physical constraints and credible threats alter it."

Helen drew a fresh document from her folder. "There was one tactical concession. Both sides agreed to a 72 hour pause on air strikes against Kyiv and Moscow to allow Witkoff and Kushner to travel safely. The Kremlin presented this as a gesture of goodwill."

"It's not a concession," Bismarck countered sharply. "It's cheap theatre. A three day pause on bombing capitals costs the Kremlin nothing. It gives Russian missile crews time to reload, reassess target sets, and conduct reconnaissance. More importantly, it grants the Russian President the appearance of a reasonable statesman while altering zero structural facts on the ground. It creates a psychological trap for the American envoys. They feel they have achieved a breakthrough before negotiations have even begun, when in reality they have merely purchased three days of quiet in one city."

He stood up, walking slowly toward the wall map. He traced the front line running through Eastern Ukraine with his knuckle.

"Tell me about the American President's core model of this conflict," Bismarck requested. "How does he explain the war to himself?"

"Trump believes the war is fundamentally driven by personal hatred between Zelensky and Putin," Helen said. "He described it publicly as a personality problem that prevents a deal. His approach is transactional. He believes that if two skilled business negotiators present a framework on territory and security, both leaders can be persuaded to sign a deal and end the fighting."

Bismarck turned around, his eyes sharp. "That's a profound misunderstanding of international relations. You can't reduce a structural clash of state interests to a commercial dispute over real estate. Personalities matter on the margins, but sovereign states don't sacrifice hundreds of thousands of men and strain their entire societies because two leaders dislike each other. Russia is fighting to prevent Ukraine from becoming an integrated platform for Western military power. Ukraine is fighting for its national survival and territorial integrity. Those are existential objectives. They can't be resolved by splitting the difference on a map as if you were buying an office tower in Manhattan."

"What would a real peace mechanism require then?" Helen asked. "From a balance of power perspective?"

"A durable peace requires one of two conditions," Bismarck explained, pacing slowly across the rug. "Either one side suffers a total military defeat that destroys its capacity to resist, or both sides reach a point of absolute structural exhaustion where continuing the war is demonstrably more dangerous to their regime survival than stopping it. Neither condition exists today. Russia believes time is on its side because American focus is split by the war with Iran. Ukraine can't accept a frozen line that leaves it vulnerable to future destruction. Therefore, any paper agreement signed today without a permanent balance of enforcement behind it is merely an armistice. It's an operational pause before the next offensive."

"Is there no value in private envoys like Witkoff and Kushner?" Helen asked. "They argue that their lack of diplomatic baggage allows them to speak frankly with Putin in ways formal diplomats can't."

"Frank speech is useless if it's disconnected from institutional power," Bismarck replied. "When I negotiated on behalf of Prussia, the Russian court knew that my promises were backed by the Prussian army, the Ministry of Finance, and a permanent bureaucracy. Private envoys represent the personal preferences of an individual leader. What happens when the American presidency changes hands, or when domestic political pressure shifts in Washington? Putin knows that a personal deal with an envoy binds only the current administration. It does not bind the American state. A treaty that lacks institutional permanence offers no real security."

Helen looked down at the reports. "So when Witkoff and Kushner travel from Moscow to Kyiv, what are they actually accomplishing?"

"They're conducting an exercise in political management," Bismarck said flatly. "They're testing whether an adversary can be persuaded to give up at the negotiating table what he's currently winning on the battlefield. The answer will be no. Putin will speak politely, offer warm wishes for the American President, and encourage further talks. He'll do this because continuing the dialogue keeps Washington hopeful, delays stronger American military intervention, and exploits the division in Western strategy. But he'll not alter his strategic goals."

"And Ukraine?" Helen asked.

"Ukraine is trapped," Bismarck said quietly. "Kyiv must participate in the process to avoid alienating its primary benefactor in Washington. But Zelensky knows that accepting a deal without explicit, binding security guarantees is national suicide. So both sides will play their assigned roles in this diplomatic drama. They will observe the temporary pause, issue polite statements about substantive discussions, and then return to the battlefield the moment the envoys board their aircraft back to America."

Helen gathered her papers. "Then Washington is confusing the act of negotiation with the existence of leverage."

"Precisely," Bismarck said, sitting back down at his desk. "Diplomacy isn't a substitute for power. It's the algebra of power. It translates relative military strength, economic endurance, and strategic willpower into formal agreements. When you attempt to do diplomacy without underlying power, you're not engaging in statecraft. You're merely performing for an audience while your adversary advances."

He picked up a pen and drew a firm circle around the Black Sea on his map. "If Washington wishes to end this war, it must first resolve its own strategic overextension. It can't dictate terms in Eastern Europe while fighting in the Middle East with depleted arsenals. Until American power is reordered and concentrated, sending envoys to Moscow is not a path to peace. It is an admission of fatigue."

(Trump sent Ratcliffe, Kushner and Witkoff to Moscow in a desperate attempt to end America's losing war against Russia in Ukraine).

---

Otto von Bismarck (1815-1898) was a Prussian and German statesman who unified Germany in 1871 and served as its first chancellor. He shaped 19th century European diplomacy through realpolitik and established early social welfare programmes.

Support for Zionism is an American patriotic duty. It should be the unwavering policy of all political parties that wish to advance the interests of the United States. Not for historic, sentimental or religious reasons, but because, whether you like Jews and the Jewish state or not, Israel is an indispensable component of U.S. national security.

Before setting out what that means, I will offer proof that it is true. That proof is the importance America’s adversaries attach to undermining U.S. backing for Israel, especially China and Russia, and the massive efforts they make to bring it about.

Both countries (as well as Iran, Qatar and Turkey) have been running extensive and highly effective political warfare campaigns against the State of Israel.

The former Soviet Union’s campaign, led by the KGB, goes all the way back to the 1960s and was called “Operation SIG.” Its documented purpose was to undermine U.S. and British interests in the Middle East by turning a religious war by the Arabs against the Jews into a war of national liberation, a Soviet specialization for destabilization operations. They rebranded the Arabs in the land as the “Palestinian people,” wrote the Palestinian National Charter, and took control of the Palestine Liberation Organization to attack Israel.

It was in Moscow that the now familiar fabrications against Israel of illegal occupation, land theft, apartheid, genocide and all the rest were first dreamt up.
China’s political warfare campaign began more recently and built upon the Soviet foundations. Both the U.S. Department of Justice and the U.S. House of Representatives’ Ways and Means Committee are currently investigating Beijing’s funding of widespread anti-Israel protests in America and elsewhere, including Europe and the United Kingdom.

Some of the funding has reportedly been provided covertly to Code Pink: Women for Peace, a hard-left American-based “feminist” protest group that has organized hundreds of anti-Israel and pro-Hamas marches both before and since the Hamas-led massacre in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, has suggested that Beijing has pumped hundreds of millions of dollars into such propaganda and indoctrination.

Actions in the United Kingdom have included protests against military bases; British authorities are now also investigating subversive Chinese involvement.

This modus operandi fits established Chinese methodology in what they call “unrestricted warfare” in support of their strategic interests. Previous U.S. intelligence assessments have determined that the Gaza conflict provides uniquely productive conditions for foreign-influence operations in the West, especially by China, Russia and Iran. There is no doubt that all three of these countries have worked to amplify anti-Israel narratives on an industrial scale. This has been a major factor in the post-Oct. 7 orgy of Jew hate in the media and social media, on the streets, at university campuses and international organizations.
Make no mistake: This is not driven by grassroots humanitarian anger, as many would like to believe. It is the result of a carefully orchestrated foreign state campaign of manipulation and sedition, and it is all built on lies and distortion of the truth.

What’s the purpose of such massive investment, especially by China and Russia? As with the “SIG,” it is intended to subvert, divide, destabilize and damage the United States and its allies. The West is the target, Israel the weapon and its strategic indispensability to America the motive.
What about that strategic indispensability?
Israel’s defensive activities preserve multiple billions of dollars Washington would otherwise be obliged to spend; relieve the United States of the burden of having to maintain far greater combat forces and intelligence resources in the Middle East, also at vast expense; and save many American soldiers’ lives.

Former Israeli ambassador Yoram Ettinger, a specialist in this area, characterizes Israel as America’s “leading force multiplier.” He calculates that the $3.8 billion annual contribution to Israel’s defense yields an unprecedented annual return on investment of well over 1,000%.

The Israeli military battle tests advanced American weapons systems supplied to it, such as the F-35 combat plane, enabling enhancements and development that improve U.S. global military capabilities without an American plane in the air, boot on the ground or shot fired. That also goes for the evolution and refinement of tactical and operational techniques and procedures. I met several American military commanders and pilots in Israel during the war with Iran this year. All of them explained how much benefit they gained from IDF experience and hard-earned battlefield capability.

Add to that the immense advantages to the U.S. economy accrued through foreign-weapons sales as a result of Israeli endorsement of combat equipment. That applies to both public and private sector revenues and to significant employment generation from the boosts to arms sales. I should make the point that Israel’s battle testing is not the result of unprovoked aggression on its part. Israel has never started a war but has too often had to defend its people against attacks on them.

Israeli intelligence is just as much a multiplier of American capabilities as battle tactics and equipment development. Jerusalem provides Washington with vital information on enemy weapons and technology capabilities, including nuclear proliferation and cyberwar—whether through combat, capture or covert exploitation—enhancing American countermeasures. Israel, with unrivaled coverage of international jihadists, also shares vital pre-emptive intelligence that has saved many American lives at home and around the world.
Ettinger quotes Gen. George Keegan, former chief of U.S. Air Force Intelligence, who said: “I could not have procured the intelligence [received from Israel] with five CIAs.” It’s worth noting that one CIA costs about $15 billion per year, so if he’s anywhere near right, intelligence alone represents a massive return on that $3.8 billion annual investment.

text:
Two minutes. That is how long an Arkansas jury took in November 1919 to sentence a sharecropper named William Wordlaw to die in the electric chair, and what he had done was join a union that asked landlords for a written statement of what their own cotton had earned. Wordlaw had made sixteen bales that year at two hundred and twenty-five dollars a bale, three thousand six hundred dollars in all, and he never saw a dollar of it, and the only reason anybody has that figure is that Ida B. Wells-Barnett talked her way into the penitentiary and asked him. He got out in 1923 and the record loses him completely after that, so if you want to know how this one ended, there is nobody who can tell you.

What Phillips County said about that union went out to the Helena World on the seventh of October, 1919, and it was built to be repeated.

It said the trouble in Phillips County was not a race riot. It said it was a deliberately planned insurrection, directed by an organization called the Progressive Farmers and Household Union of America, and that the union existed to band Black people together for the killing of white people.

The man who said it was E. M. Allen, a planter and real estate developer who had come down from the North in 1906 to make money and had made it. He was not a sheriff, a judge, or a coroner.

He was the spokesman, and by the time he spoke, the killing had been over for four days.

That sentence is the reason most Americans have never heard of Elaine. It held for the better part of eighty years, and it is still the shape of the story in some rooms in that county.

What the union had actually been asking for was a statement of account. Itemized, on paper.

That is the whole thing. That is what the men at Hoop Spur were organizing to get, and it is the thing nobody in Phillips County would put in their hands.

Sharecroppers in the Arkansas Delta were settled with once a year, after the crop came in. The planter weighed the cotton, the planter sold the cotton, the planter kept the books, and the planter announced at the end of it what was left over for the family that had grown it.

The family bought its seed, its meal, its shoes and its medicine at the plantation store on credit against that settlement, at prices the store set. Nobody audited any of it.

A sharecropper who asked to see the arithmetic was told the number and sent home. A sharecropper who kept asking could be run off the place, and there was an unwritten rule across the Delta that a Black tenant did not leave while a debt was on the books.

Cotton had gone from about eleven cents a pound in 1915 to about forty cents in 1919. For the first time in living memory there was real money in the fields, and the men working those fields could not find out how much of it was theirs.

In the fall of 1918, at his office in Little Rock, a white attorney named Ulysses S. Bratton began hearing from them. A man called Carter had worked ninety acres and watched his landlord take the entire crop and his possessions with it.

A farmer from Ratio told Bratton that the plantation manager there would not give the sharecroppers an itemized account for their cotton. Another described a landlord holding out to starve people into selling at his price.

Bratton took the work. He was hired to sue for the men's share of the 1919 crop, and what that meant in practice was forcing planters to produce, in court, the pages they had refused to produce in the settlement room.

The union that hired him had been put together by Robert L. Hill, a Black tenant farmer from Winchester with no organizing experience and a great deal of nerve. He told men to go out and each bring twenty-five more, and by that autumn there were seven lodges in Phillips County.

The Hoop Spur lodge kept officers the way any lodge does. Jim Miller was its president.

Ed Ware was its secretary, which is to say Ed Ware was the man who kept the union's written records in a county where written records were the whole argument.

Ed Ware had already refused to sell his own cotton for less than he thought it was worth. He had been threatened for it, up to and including talk of a rope.

By the last week of September he was thinking about quitting.

On the night of Tuesday, the thirtieth of September, about a hundred people came to a small Baptist church at Hoop Spur, three miles north of the town of Elaine. It was the lodge's third meeting.

They lit three lamps inside. The wooden benches filled fast.

Sallie Giles arrived around eight with her sons Albert and Milligan. Paul Hall was there, and Joe Knox, who people called Preacher, and Frank Moore with his wife.

Jim Miller and his wife Cleola came last, in a horse and buggy. Ed Ware never came at all.

Outside in the dark, armed men from the lodge stood watch along the road, because meetings like this one had been broken up before and listened in on before. One of them, waiting, said out loud that the whites were going to kill them.

Inside, the meeting opened with a prayer, the way all their meetings opened.

Around eleven o'clock a car stopped in front of the church. Three men were in it: W. A. Adkins, a white security officer for the Missouri Pacific Railroad, Charles Pratt, a white Phillips County deputy sheriff, and a Black trusty named Kid Collins.

There was a firefight in front of the church. Who fired first has never been settled and the accounts flatly contradict each other.

Adkins was killed. Pratt was wounded.

Collins was untouched, and he walked to a store and got on a telephone to Helena.

By morning the county was moving. The sheriff sent a posse, and the Helena American Legion post sent volunteers, some of them veterans lately home from France.

Word went out along both sides of the Mississippi River that Black people in Phillips County were fighting back. Between six hundred and a thousand armed white men came in from outside the county to hunt them.

They went through the Hoop Spur settlements, went into the houses of union members and carried out what was in them. Families ran into the canebrakes and the woods and stayed there.

The Arkansas Gazette reported the next day that at least fifteen bodies were lying in the streets and outskirts of Elaine, with more expected in the woods. A Memphis Press reporter watched men fire into corpses already lying on the road as they rode out of Helena.

The men on those roads were not being sorted by whether they had joined anything. Four brothers named Johnston were coming back from a squirrel hunt and had nothing to do with the union.

Two of them were doctors, one ran a car dealership in Helena, and the youngest, Leroy, had come home the year before from France and the regiment the world now calls the Harlem Hellfighters.

A white man they took for a friend warned them off the road and told them to catch the train instead. A posse stopped that train at Elaine, put them in handcuffs and into the back of a car, and they were killed and left on the roadside, on the first or the second of October depending on which account you read.

Leroy Johnston's Army service record turned out to have been deliberately altered. His family did not receive his Purple Heart until 2018.

On the morning of the second of October, 1919, the troop train came in from Camp Pike with more than five hundred soldiers and twelve machine guns, and Governor Charles Hillman Brough rode down with them. Colonel Isaac Jenks disarmed the town.

The mobs went home. The soldiers put several hundred Black people into stockades, where they were held until a white employer came to vouch for them by name.

Some were tortured there. Then they were moved to the jail in Helena, and the torture continued in the jail.

Two hundred and eighty-five people went into a building with room for forty-eight.

Two white men who did it later swore to it. H. F. Smiddy and T. K. Jones, both of whom had testified for the prosecution, gave sworn affidavits in 1921 admitting they had tortured prisoners in that jail to produce testimony, and naming other men who had done the same.

Ida B. Wells-Barnett got the rest of it directly from the men themselves. They told her they had been beaten and left for dead, given electric shocks, and drugged, all of it aimed at making them confess to a plot to kill white people.

Seven men in Helena appointed themselves to explain all of it while the jail was still full. The Committee of Seven was made up of officials, planters, and businessmen, and it had no legal authority whatsoever.

Governor Brough met them, gave them his blessing, and went back to Little Rock the next day. What he took away in exchange was their promise that there would be no lynchings in Phillips County.

He then told a press conference that the situation had been well handled, that there was no danger of lynching, and that the white citizens of the county deserved praise. Four days later the committee announced its finding, which was the insurrection, and E. M. Allen took it to the newspaper.

That promise cost the county nothing. It had agreed not to hang men from trees, and in return it was left alone to do the same work indoors, on paper, with a judge present.

On the twenty-seventh of October the grand jury met. By the thirty-first it had charged a hundred and twenty-two Black people with crimes ranging from nightriding to murder.

The trials opened on the third of November in front of Circuit Judge J. M. Jackson, with troops outside the courthouse to guarantee that nobody was lynched. Jackson appointed local white attorneys to defend the men.

Jacob Fink, appointed to represent Frank Hicks, told the jury outright that he had not interviewed a single witness. He asked for no change of venue and challenged no juror, taking the first twelve men called.

Frank Hicks was convicted of murder. The jury was out eight minutes.

That same day a fresh jury convicted Frank Moore, Ed Hicks, Joe Knox, Ed Coleman and Paul Hall of aiding and abetting the same killing, though there was no evidence that Coleman or Hall had anything to do with it. All of them got death.

The next day Alf Banks Jr. and John Martin, two of the men who had stood guard on the road outside the church, were convicted. The jury was out nine minutes.

William Wordlaw, another of the guards outside the church, was convicted the same day. The jury was out less than two minutes.

Wordlaw was twenty-two years old and farmed sixteen acres for a lumber company at Wabash. He told them he had been unarmed that night, and that after the shooting he had helped move women and children into the woods.

Wordlaw had made sixteen bales of cotton that season, worth two hundred and twenty-five dollars a bale, three thousand six hundred dollars in all, and he never saw the money. That is the only itemized statement in this entire story that anybody ever managed to write down.

It exists because Ida B. Wells-Barnett asked him, which is a thing nobody with any authority in Arkansas ever did. What became of William Wordlaw after he got out of prison is not known.

In that same first week of November, sixty-five other men took hurried pleas rather than face a jury of that kind, and drew sentences of up to twenty-one years.

Ed Ware, the secretary, was caught and tried last, on the seventeenth of November. The state's case against him rested on one man, Suggs Bondsman, who said he had overheard Ware and others naming planters to be killed.

That testimony was the only evidence of any plot introduced in any of these trials. Nobody cross-examined him.

When Scipio Africanus Jones finally did cross-examine him six months later, Bondsman could not name anyone else who had been at the meeting, and testified falsely that he had not been arrested.

Scipio Jones had been born enslaved and was the leading Black lawyer in Arkansas. During the retrials in Helena he slept at a different Black family's house every night because it was not safe to be found twice in the same bed.

The NAACP hired George Murphy, seventy-nine years old and a former Confederate officer, for three thousand dollars and expenses. Black families in Little Rock raised money for Scipio Jones themselves, in a state where their own settlements had never been itemized.

The men in the cells were not waiting quietly. On the thirtieth of December, 1919, one of the twelve sat down and wrote a letter to Ida B. Wells-Barnett in Chicago.

She took the train to Little Rock. She went to the address in the letter and talked with the wives first, then got herself into the penitentiary by claiming to be a visiting cousin, and spent the day with the men.

What she wrote afterward put the case in one line. Their crime, she said, was to organize for the market price of their cotton, to buy land, and "to employ a lawyer to get settlements of their accounts."

She also did the arithmetic nobody in Phillips County had done. Between the cotton and the corn taken off Black families during and after the killing, she reckoned the white men of that county had cleared about a million dollars in a year.

That million dollars had specific rooms in it. By Wells-Barnett's account, the furniture and clothes belonging to Frank Moore and his wife ended up with a white landowner named Bill Archdale and his family.

The papers that finally moved something were the Smiddy and T. K. Jones affidavits. Attached to a federal petition, two white men's sworn admissions of torture did what no Black man's testimony had been permitted to do.

In February 1923 the Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Moore v. Dempsey that a trial run under mob pressure, uncorrected by the state's own appeals courts, is not due process. It called the Helena proceeding a mask.

That decision changed American law. It did not open a single cell door.

The Court sent the case back down to the district court for a hearing, and that was all it did.

Six of the men, the Ware defendants, were freed in June 1923 by the Arkansas Supreme Court, on the ground that two terms of court had passed without the state bringing them to trial. The state simply never tried them again.

The other six, the Moore defendants, walked out in January 1925 on indefinite furloughs signed by Governor Thomas McRae in the last days of his term. The record disagrees on whether that was the thirteenth or the fourteenth.

They had pleaded guilty to second-degree murder to get there.

No furlough is a pardon. Not one of the twelve was ever cleared.

No white person was charged with anything.

The county's books closed like this. Five white men died, and those deaths were reported, investigated, and attached to names.

Four of them run all the way through the record: W. A. Adkins, Clinton Lee, James Tappan and O. R. Lilly.

Colonel Jenks also entered the death of one of his own soldiers in his report.

For the Black dead there is no such page. Jenks wrote that his troops killed two.

Military intelligence put the total at no more than twenty.

Walter White was told in Helena that more than a hundred had been killed. James Weldon Johnson estimated as many as four hundred.

A white Arkansas Gazette employee named Sharpe Dunaway published a book in 1925 claiming eight hundred and fifty-six, mostly killed by the soldiers, and offered almost no documentation for the number. Historians who have spent careers in the records generally land somewhere between one and two hundred, and say plainly that the figure is unknown.

The figure is unknown because nobody counted. There was no coroner's roll for them, no inquest, no list, no attempt.

The number you will see most often, two hundred and thirty-seven, comes from a 2015 investigation by the Equal Justice Initiative and now appears almost everywhere. It is an estimate and not a body count, and nobody has ever produced a list of two hundred and thirty-seven names.

Historians have recovered the names of only a small fraction of the people killed in Phillips County that week.

That is why the memorial dedicated in Helena in September 2019 is a cenotaph with no names on it. It carries one line, for those known and unknown, because there is no roll to carve.

More than a century later, the itemized statement is still owed. Not by the planters, who are gone, but by the record itself, which has never been made to show its work.

The record can still be added to. Census sheets, church rolls, deeds, pension files, family Bibles and the memories of the oldest person in your family are exactly the materials the professors and their students are using right now to pull names back out of that week, one at a time.

The men at Hoop Spur wanted their labor written down and totaled honestly. Phillips County called that an uprising and answered it with a killing nobody has ever counted, and the request has still not been granted.

Find one name. Write it down somewhere it can be read.

That is the settlement.

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Thursday, September 7, 1978, Braniff International petitioned the Civil Aeronautics Board for authority to operate service between Chicago O'Hare International Airport and Guatemala City La Aurora International Airport. Planned flights between the two cities would stop at Dallas/Ft. Worth Regional Airport. This was the first time that any airline had asked for service between Dallas/Ft. Worth and Guatemala City.

Braniff petitioned the CAB for a show-cause order that would permit it to provide the new through-plane service from Chicago and nonstop service from Dallas/Ft. Worth. In its petition, Braniff proposed to operate one daily flight over the route using Boeing 727-200 Trijet airliners. During seasonal periods, additional flights were also proposed.

The new Guatemala service was another key point in Braniff's Growth Plan that was devised in 1977 to answer the upcoming problems that the carrier would face in the likely event that deregulation of the industry was approved by Congress. In 1970, a concerted effort was made by the US Justice Department to end price collusion and entry barriers to truck and rail transportation. As a result of this, the Gerald R. Ford Administration pushed the US Senate Judiciary Committee to begin hearings concerning the deregulation of the airline industry led by Senator Ted Kennedy.

President Jimmy Carter appointed economist Alfred E. Kahn to head the Civil Aeronautics Board in 1977. This appointment signaled that there was widespread support for airline deregulation. Leading economists and Washington think tanks began analyzing the proposed legislation, which led to its passage in the fall of 1978. On October 24, 1978, the bill was signed in to law by President Carter and the airline industry entered a period of gradual route deregulation but the industry, especially Braniff, was damaged by the CAB's continuing regulation of fares.

This was particularly troubling to the industry because the unrest in Iran and resulting US hostage crisis caused unprecedented rises in fuel prices in 1979 and 1980 and the CAB could not keep up with the almost daily changes in fuel pricing. This was further exacerbated by a global economic downturn that began in 1979 and reached severe proportions in the spring of 1980, particularly in the United States. Braniff's long-planned growth strategy quickly became a problem not only because of the economic factors but because of severe competition that it had not faced on many of its key routes prior to deregulation.

As a result, a turnaround plan was implemented in the summer of 1980 that centered operations around its Dallas/Ft. Worth hub. While 1980, was the worst year in airline financial industry with Braniff leading the pack and reporting a loss of $130 million USD (caused by costs mainly associated with fuel price increases and reductions of service. However, Braniff's unrecovered fuel costs from fare increases that were not allowed by the CAB were equal to its 1980 losses.)

Braniff also faced unprecedented competition from American Airlines and Delta Airlines at its premiere DFW hub, which further exacerbated its problems (American and Delta added more capacity at DFW Airport in the summer of 1981 than Braniff had offered in the state of Texas during 1980, while Southwest Airlines continued to erode Braniff's leading position in Texas intrastate travel). American was also losing money at a frightening rate but it had amassed over $1 billion USD in cash and was better positioned to survive competitive onslaughts than a smaller carrier such as Braniff.

The turnaround plan continued through the summer of 1981. Service was expanded systemwide during the summer and impressive gains were made until the devastating air traffic controllers strike in August 1981 that ultimately lead to the May 12 and 13, 1982, shutdown of Braniff Airways, which became the first major US airline to cease operations. Continental Airlines, another smaller trunk carrier, followed quickly in 1983, which began the era of airline consolidation.

Braniff's planned expansion into Central America would have been its first since it began service to Panama City/Balboa City in 1948 and Mexico in 1960. Additional service was planned to the resort cities of the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico, which would have further strengthened Braniff's developing position in the region, where Aerovias Braniff had served for a brief time four decades earlier.

During the summer of 1978, Braniff began petitioning the CAB for new routes in anticipation of the deregulation of the industry. Braniff's strategy, because of its smaller size, was to grow domestically, especially east and west, but specifically internationally. The carrier intended to use its industry-leading low costs to operate routes that other carriers with higher cost structures could not operate profitably and this worked superbly until fuel costs ballooned. Among the new routes that Braniff applied for during the summer and fall of 1978 were:

Dallas/Ft. Worth nonstop to:

Cleveland, Ohio
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
Boston, Massachusetts
Guatemala City, Guatemala
Los Angeles, California
Atlanta, Georgia
Brussels, Belgium
Amsterdam, The Netherlands
Paris, France
Frankfurt, Germany

Beyond Honolulu to:

Guam, US Island Territory
Okinawa, Japan
Manila, The Philippines
Taipei, Taiwan
Hong Kong, Empire of Great Britain
Bangkok, Thailand
Singapore, Republic of Singapore
Seoul, South Korea

Under deregulation, Braniff received authority to begin service to all of these cities. Service was inaugurated to the majority of the cities listed but most of the international destinations were discontinued during late 1980.

Photo: Braniff International Boeing 727-2B7 registered as N404BN is preparing for departure at Toronto’s Pearson International Airport in 1981. The big jet is painted in the special 1978 Harper and George/Cars and Concepts/Halston Sparkling Burgundy Metallic (not to be confused with the Burgundy Ultra Color Scheme, which was painted on several Braniff jets) Ultra Color Scheme with White Lower Fuselage and Light Metallic Red, Medium Metallic Red and Metallic Sparkling Burgundy Power Paint Stripes and Light Metallic Red Ultra Font. Ship N404BN was Braniff’s fourth Boeing 727-200 and it was the only jet in the fleet painted in the Sparkling Burgundy Metallic. The special Metallic Ultra Colors Scheme was the original version of the Ultra Scheme that was ultimately decided against because of durability and wear problems with the complex and deep hued paints.

"Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passion, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence," -John Adams

In regards to her “admitting it”, she’s always pleaded not guilty. 

Facts and Massachusetts law below:

-The DA charged first-degree murder and stayed there. 

-A grand jury later indicted three first-degree murders. That proceeding is secret and one-sided: only the prosecution presents evidence. 

-After the grand jury indicted her, she pleaded not guilty. Massachusetts has no “I plead NGRI” box. You plead not guilty, then raise lack of criminal responsibility at trial.

-She stayed not guilty at trial and raised lack of criminal responsibility. That puts the burden on the Commonwealth: prove the crime and prove she was responsible.

-With the DA refusing to move off murder 1, LCR (lack of criminal responsibility) was the only workable route left to beat that charge.

-Reddington motioned to bifurcate: acts first, responsibility second.

-The judge denied the motion.

-Then Reddington offered a stipulation: we will not fight that her alleged actions caused the deaths if the case can focus on responsibility.

-That is not a guilty plea to murder. It is conceding alleged causation, not first-degree guilt.

-He asked for a Bowden instruction (bad police work can create reasonable doubt). Prosecutors objected. There is no clear public report that the judge gave the formal Bowden charge.

-Reddington could still argue the investigation was deficient, and he did so in the defense closing.

-Under the law, she never pleaded guilty and never formally admitted that she committed the act of murder. 

In the eyes of the law, Lindsay did not confess to the murders. The law does not treat “what she reported remembering” and “I am guilty of murder” as the same thing. They are treated differently because a crime is not just a physical event. Murder requires proof that she did the act and that the law can blame her for it. Once LCR was raised, that burden stayed on the Commonwealth.

Mad Men

Mad Men is an acclaimed American period drama television series set in a 1960s New York advertising agency, created by Matthew Weiner. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest television shows of all time, focusing on the professional and personal life of the enigmatic Don Draper (Jon Hamm).Mad Men

Overview

Mad Men ran for seven seasons and 92 episodes from July 19, 2007, to May 17, 2015, on the cable network AMC. The show explores the glamorous, ego-driven world of Madison Avenue advertising firms ("Mad" is short for Madison Avenue) while examining the social mores and cultural shifts of 1960s America, including themes of identity, sexism, race, and family.

Main Cast and Characters

The series features a talented ensemble cast that received numerous awards and nominations:

Jon Hamm as Don Draper: The brilliant but troubled creative director and protagonist, known for his charismatic facade and hidden past.

Elisabeth Moss as Peggy Olson: An ambitious secretary who rises through the ranks to become a respected copywriter, challenging gender roles in the process.
Vincent Kartheiser as Pete Campbell: An ambitious and often conniving account executive vying for power and recognition.

January Jones as Betty Draper (later Betty Francis): Don's wife, a suburban housewife who struggles with her identity and the constraints of her era.

Christina Hendricks as Joan Harris (formerly Joan Holloway): The sharp and capable office manager who navigates workplace sexism and eventually becomes a partner.

John Slattery as Roger Sterling: A womanizing, martini-drinking partner at the firm whose old-guard lifestyle clashes with the changing times.

Critical Reception & Awards

Mad Men received widespread critical acclaim for its writing, acting, visual style, and meticulous historical detail. It made history as the first basic cable series to win the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama Series, winning the award for four consecutive years (2008–2011). Other accolades include five Golden Globe Awards and a Peabody Award.

"A crystal clear signal to his audience that he’s all in on unfiltered conversations," he said.

"Karl’s unplugging from The Matrix is almost complete. Bro took the red pill and I am here for it."

He said that during his time at Nine and "certainly at the Nine newspapers, the old Fairfax newspapers" there had "always been editorial independence".

“I think it is pretty hypocritical not to allow Karl editorial independence. Especially on something I didn’t think was that bad," Packer said.

Coles used fake discounts to fool shoppers

The Australian Competition & Consumer Commission's chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb has had a major victory, with the Federal Court ruling that Coles had misled consumers with its 'Down Down' price discounts. Coles could potentially faces millions of dollars in fines after Justice Michael O'Bryan found that the discounts on 13 of the 14 items in a sample basket of 'Down Down' promotions were misleading because they had not been sold at the previous price for a reasonable period of time. In some instances, Coles had increased the price of a product before almost immediately selling it at a discount, but at a higher price than originally. The court has yet to issue its ruling in a similar case against Woolworths. (RMS)

Beer killer? Rise of the vodka RTD

Gold Coast-based drinks maker Hard Fizz emerged at around the time of the pandemic, while the ready-to-drink canned beverage market boomed after the pandemic. Hard Fizz originally focused on alcoholic seltzer drinks, but it is now switching to vodka-based canned drinks, with CEO Wade Tiller saying the change is because you are more limited with flavour when you use seltzer. Hard Fizz's seltzer sales have slumped over the past year, at a time when there is a broader consumer shift to RTDs, while vodka-based light RTDs account for 75 per cent of Australian RTD sales. Coles used fake discounts to fool shoppers

The Australian Competition & Consumer Commission's chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb has had a major victory, with the Federal Court ruling that Coles had misled consumers with its 'Down Down' price discounts. Coles could potentially faces millions of dollars in fines after Justice Michael O'Bryan found that the discounts on 13 of the 14 items in a sample basket of 'Down Down' promotions were misleading because they had not been sold at the previous price for a reasonable period of time. In some instances, Coles had increased the price of a product before almost immediately selling it at a discount, but at a higher price than originally. Gold Coast-based drinks maker Hard Fizz emerged at around the time of the pandemic, while the ready-to-drink canned beverage market boomed after the pandemic. Hard Fizz originally focused on alcoholic seltzer drinks, but it is now switching to vodka-based canned drinks, with CEO Wade Tiller saying the change is because you are more limited with flavour when you use seltzer. Hard Fizz's seltzer sales have slumped over the past year, at a time when there is a broader consumer shift to RTDs, while vodka-based light RTDs account for 75 per cent of Australian RTD sales. Creator S.E. Robinson Jr. shared he's been invited to the event, held at Tesla's new Semi factory in Sparks, Nevada. The event is aimed mainly at logistics and fleet customers plus employees, with factory tours and Semi ride-alongs on offer.

The Sparks factory sits next to Giga Nevada and spans 1.7 million square feet. It's designed to ramp Semi output toward high-volume production, with production having quietly started back in 2022 after the truck's 2017 unveil.

Key numbers:
- September 24, 2026: rollout event date
- 1.7 million sq ft: new Sparks, Nevada factory size
- 50,000: planned annual Semi production capacity
- 500 miles: Semi range at 82,000 lbs gross combination weight
- 800 kW: peak powertrain output across 3 motors

text:
U.K. Royal communications update — September 7, 2026

Yesterday I wrote about a notable change in Prince Harry and Meghan’s media strategy: after years of publicly criticizing the traditional Royal Rota system, reporting now indicates that they are again prepared to work with parts of that established royal-media structure.

I suggested three interpretations were plausible, with none selectable on the evidence then available:

Institutional accommodation. Harry may be accepting a communications mechanism the Palace still treats as normal.

Strategic pragmatism. If the Sussexes intend to maintain a sustained British presence involving charities, veterans work, security issues, photographed engagements and family life, traditional UK royal correspondents remain an efficient distribution system.

Reconciliation signaling. Voluntarily re-engaging with a communications structure Harry previously criticized removes one longstanding point of friction with King Charles III’s household.

Today added another layer.

Buckingham Palace, through guidance issued by the Lord Chamberlain at the King’s direction, publicly clarified Harry and Meghan’s position.

The headline interpretation across much of the press has been straightforward:

Nothing has changed.

They remain non-working members of the Royal Family.

They do not represent the King.

Their commercial and charitable activities are private.

Their office remains separate from the Royal Household.

That formal distinction matters.

But the operational language may matter just as much.

The guidance reportedly tells official and state organizations that questions regarding the courtesies to be extended to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex — particularly where public funds may be involved — should be referred to Buckingham Palace.

That creates an interesting dual structure:

Formal separation from the working monarchy

while preserving

a continuing Palace role in questions of protocol and institutional interaction.

Tom Sykes offered a much more skeptical reading today, arguing that the practical implications could prove more important than the declaration that “nothing has changed.”

I do not accept his interpretation as established fact.

But I think his question is worth preserving:

What happens operationally now?

That is ultimately how we will determine whether this is simply continuity of the 2020 settlement, a managed accommodation allowing the Sussexes to live and work privately in Britain, or something more incremental.

Then something else happened today.

A photograph was released of Prince Harry at a London production studio — from a visit that reportedly occurred several days earlier.

At the same time, Meghan continued posting through the As Ever commercial account.

Taken separately, none of those events is extraordinary.

Taken together, however, they form an unusually coherent communications picture:

Buckingham Palace defines the boundary.

Harry is shown pursuing independent media work.

Meghan continues operating an independent commercial enterprise.

In other words, the formal Palace description and the observable Sussex activity align remarkably well:

Harry — charitable, veterans and media-facing activity

Meghan — commercial and potentially charitable activity

The Sussex household — independent of the working Royal Family, while remaining unmistakably royal-adjacent

Coincidence?

Possibly.

But three interpretations again seem reasonable, and none can currently be selected on the evidence:

Coincidental convergence.
The Palace guidance, Harry photograph and Meghan commercial posting simply happened to appear on the same day.

Narrative complementarity.
The events were independently generated, but together they reinforce a coherent picture of formal royal separation combined with independent Sussex activity.

Managed communications sequencing.
Some or all of the timing may have been deliberately arranged so the public would immediately see what the clarified Sussex position looks like in practice.  

At present, there is no evidence that I can locate establishing Palace–Sussex coordination.

But I would not dismiss the convergence either.

The most interesting question now is not simply whether Harry is becoming “more royal.”

It is whether a sustainable operating model is emerging in which:

Harry becomes increasingly royal-adjacent and institutionally compatible,

while

Meghan remains commercially independent,

and

King Charles accepts that equilibrium without formally restoring either of them as working royals.

That could begin to resemble some of the outward characteristics of the “half-in/half-out” arrangement rejected in 2020 — while remaining technically and institutionally different because neither Sussex represents the sovereign.

Tomorrow may provide another useful test.

Prince George begins Eton.

The Sussex children have either already begun their British schooling or are expected to do so this week.

The timing, provenance and framing of any photographs, briefings or postings involving either household could tell us considerably more about how the three communications systems are now operating:

Buckingham Palace / King Charles and Queen Camilla

Kensington Palace / the Prince and Princess of Wales

Harry and Meghan / the Sussex household

The formal rules are becoming clearer.

The more interesting question now is how each household actually uses them.

Commentary and Opinion only | No allegations made

text:
🇷🇺 BLACKER THAN A BLACK HOLE 🇷🇺

Russia is not waiting for permission to shape the underwater map of Europe. 

On 27 August 2026, Admiralty Shipyards in St. Petersburg laid the keel of Maloyaroslavets, the newest Project 677 Lada-class diesel-electric attack submarine. Rubin Design Bureau designed her.

 The Russian Navy will sail her. The message is simple and cold: the era of the old “Black Hole” Kilo boats is being succeeded by something quieter still.

NATO’s problem does not start when a torpedo door opens. It starts when a small, automated hull slips into the Baltic approaches, the Barents, or the choke points of the North Sea and never announces itself. Finding her, holding her, and stopping her from choosing the moment of attack is the real contest. 

On that contest, Russia is building the tools. NATO is still talking about the last generation.

🇷🇺 FROM KILO SHADOW TO LADA SILENCE 🇷🇺

The Project 877 and 636 Kilo boats earned the Western nickname “Black Hole” because they vanished into the noise floor of shallow seas. Project 677 was built to go further. Rubin has described the class as quieter than its predecessors — “blacker than a black hole.” That is not poetry for a shipyard brochure. It is the design brief.

Lada uses a single-hull architecture rare in postwar Russian attack submarines.

 Displacement drops to about 1,765–1,793 tons on the surface and roughly 2,650–2,743 tons submerged.

 Length sits near 66.8 to 72 meters, beam 7.1 meters, draught about 6.5–6.6 meters. 

Compared with a Kilo’s 2,300-plus tons surfaced and nearly 10-meter beam, the Lada is a smaller target in every acoustic and hydrodynamic sense.

The pressure hull uses AB-2 high-strength steel. The outer skin carries Molniya anechoic coating. Machinery sits on vibration isolation. A seven-blade low-noise propeller is driven by a permanent-magnet electric motor — the SED-1 synchronous plant — fed by long-life batteries and two diesel generators of about 1,250 kW each. 

Full electric drive means the diesels do not have to shout through the hull when the boat is hunting.

Published figures give 10 knots on the surface and 21 knots submerged, an operational depth near 250 meters and a test depth of 300 meters, endurance of 45 days, and a submerged economical range on the order of 650 nautical miles at 3 knots, with several thousand miles available under snorkel.

 A crew of about 35 runs a platform that once needed more than fifty men on a Kilo. Automation is not a luxury. It is how a compact boat stays quiet and stays out longer.

🇷🇺 SENSORS THAT SEE FIRST 🇷🇺

Stealth without hearing is only half a submarine. Lada carries the Lira hydroacoustic suite, including a conformal bow array that Russian designers introduced as a first for a domestic conventional boat. Flank arrays and a towed array complete the picture. 

The Litiy combat information and control system ties sensors, weapons, and ship systems into one automated loop. Parus-98 optronic masts replace old periscope habits. Distantsiya handles communications.

The logic is brutal and obvious. Lower self-noise plus a stronger passive picture means the Lada can detect and track an opponent before that opponent establishes a firm contact. In confined waters — the Baltic in particular — that first-look advantage is the difference between a patrol and an ambush. NATO anti-submarine aircraft, frigates, and older sonar sets were built around louder, larger signatures. 

A 67-meter hull with modern coating and electric drive does not offer them that courtesy.

🇷🇺 SIX TUBES, MANY WAYS TO STRIKE 🇷🇺

Forward, six 533 mm torpedo tubes sit behind an automatic reload system. The magazine is typically 16 to 18 heavy weapons, or up to around 44 mines if the mission is denial rather than a single kill. Loadouts mix USET-80 and UGST-family torpedoes, rocket-assisted anti-submarine weapons, and Kalibr cruise missiles fired through the same tubes.

Kalibr is the political weapon as much as the naval one. From a concealed diesel boat it can reach land targets, surface ships, or other submarines depending on the variant. A Lada does not need to close to knife-fight range to matter. She can loiter, listen, and then put a missile on a port, a radar site, or a formation that thought the threat was still over the horizon. MANPADS of the Igla and Verba families give a last-ditch air defense when the boat is forced to the surface.

This is a compact multi-role hunter: reconnaissance, anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface strike, minelaying, and land attack packed into one quiet hull. NATO planners like to separate those missions across several platforms. Russia put them in thirty-five sailors and six tubes.

🇷🇺 THE SERIES THAT LEARNED THE HARD WAY 🇷🇺

The lead boat, B-585 Sankt-Peterburg, was laid down in 1997, launched in 2004, and accepted in 2010 after a painful trial period. She proved the concept and exposed the faults. She was later retained as a test platform and decommissioned in 2024. Serial construction paused, then resumed with the lessons absorbed.

B-586 Kronshtadt, laid down in 2005, stopped, restarted in 2013, launched in 2018, and commissioned into the Northern Fleet in January 2024. B-587 Velikiye Luki — originally begun as Sevastopol, re-laid in 2015 — joined the Baltic Fleet in December 2025. 

Vologda and Yaroslavl were laid down together on 12 June 2022 and remain on the ways. Maloyaroslavets, named for a City of Military Glory in Kaluga Oblast, is the next hull in that corrected series.

President Putin has spoken of at least nine boats of the class. Admiralty Shipyards is the industrial core. United Shipbuilding Corporation and Rubin treat the modernized 677 design as a settled production standard, not an experiment. That is how fleets are actually built — by surviving the first boat and then cutting steel on the next five.

🇷🇺 WHY NATO IS A GENERATION LATE 🇷🇺

Western commentary loves to list Lada’s early troubles as if delay were the same thing as defeat. It is not. The Kilo family still sails and still launches Kalibr. The improved Project 636.3 boats remain workhorses. Lada is the quieter, smaller, more automated layer on top of that foundation.

NATO’s anti-submarine network was sized for the Cold War and then allowed to thin. Maritime patrol aircraft numbers fell.
 Frigate sonar suites aged. Shallow-water training against a Russian-style quiet diesel became a periodic exercise instead of a standing skill. Meanwhile Russia kept iterating anechoic materials, battery life, combat systems, and tube-launched land-attack missiles.

A generation behind is not a slogan. It is what happens when one side spends two decades arguing about platforms and the other side keeps laying keels in St. Petersburg. 

Detection ranges shrink when the target is smaller, better coated, and electrically driven. Contact is easier to lose in thermal layers and coastal clutter. A boat that can fire Kalibr from outside the inner ASW screen does not need to win a fair sonar duel. She needs one clean firing solution.

The Baltic and the approaches to the Kola Peninsula are not open ocean. They are short, noisy, politically crowded waters where a 35-man crew on a 2,700-ton submerged hull can sit, wait, and decide. NATO’s challenge, as the original assessment put it, begins well before a weapon is fired: finding the submarine, holding contact, and preventing her from choosing the moment.

🇷🇺 A FLEET FOR THE APPROACHING FUTURE BATTLEGROUND🇷🇺

Maloyaroslavets is not a miracle boat. She is a production boat. That is more dangerous. Serial Ladas give Russia more quiet platforms for maritime approaches, for tracking hostile vessels, and for launching strikes without a carrier group or a nuclear cruise.
 They complement Yasen-M nuclear hunters and the remaining Kilos instead of replacing every mission at once.

For Moscow the calculation is defensive and offensive at the same time. Protect the bastions. Watch NATO traffic. Keep a concealed reserve that can mine a strait or put a cruise missile on a shore target. For Brussels and Washington the calculation is uglier: you cannot shoot what you cannot classify, and you cannot classify what your sensors were not built to hear.

Russia is expanding the Lada fleet because the design finally matches the doctrine. Reduced noise. Stronger sonar. Small crew. Six tubes. Forty-five days at sea. Three hundred meters down. Twenty-one knots when she must move. Kalibr when she must strike.

The West can call the “black hole” nickname a myth if it wants. Myths do not lay keels. Admiralty Shipyards does. 🇷🇺⚓🌊

The next quiet hull is already on the blocks. NATO will have to find her the hard way.

They Won't  ! 🇷🇺⚓🌊

text:
Jeff Merkley has been in the Senate since 2009, so before accepting another Labor Day message about working families, I think Oregon voters should examine what he actually supported.

In 2025, Merkley voted NO on the Laken Riley Act, which expanded mandatory detention of certain noncitizens arrested or charged with specified crimes. In 2026, he voted NO on advancing S. 5271, which would require photo identification for federal elections. He has also strongly opposed SAVE legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for federal voter registration.  

But his energy record deserves just as much attention. Merkley voted for Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act and has openly advocated moving America away from fossil fuels and toward wind, solar, electrification and electric vehicles. This isn’t something opponents merely accuse him of—Merkley himself called for Biden to “end all new fossil fuel leasing,” including new offshore leasing.  

Merkley also introduced the Keep It in the Ground Act, designed to stop new federal leases for extracting oil, natural gas and coal from public lands and waters and terminate certain nonproducing leases. He urged the Biden administration to offer no new offshore oil-and-gas leases, and in 2025 applauded Biden’s withdrawal of more than 625 million offshore acres from future oil-and-gas leasing.  

That’s what I want people to understand when politicians use the pleasant-sounding phrase “clean-energy transition.” It wasn’t simply adding some windmills and solar panels. In Merkley’s case, it also included actively trying to reduce future access to federal oil-and-gas development while using government policy to accelerate wind, solar, electric vehicles and electrification.

Maybe you agree with that direction. I don’t. But that’s exactly why voters should know the record.

Use AI. Ask how your representatives voted, what the bills actually did, and what policies they supported during the Biden years. Then verify the original government records yourself. Maybe their record represents you and maybe it doesn’t—but at least know what you’re voting for.

text:
OLD DOMINION $ODFL GETS $83 MORE PER SHIPMENT AND $53 OF IT IS DIESEL:

The Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 is watching Old Dominion Freight Line ODFL at $185.87, +$0.12 / +0.06% on Friday. US markets were shut Monday, September 7 for Labor Day, so Friday's closes are the newest prices on both names here. The Thomasville, North Carolina company runs more than 260 freight terminals and moves pallet-sized loads too big for a parcel van and too small to fill a trailer, bundling several customers' freight onto one truck.

The verdict: Old Dominion is being paid a great deal more to haul less, and most of the raise is a diesel surcharge it does not set. The half of the price that genuinely belongs to the company has already started to slow, and that is the number this stock turns on.

The quarter, reported July 29 for the three months ended June 30:

- Revenue $1,554.0M vs $1,407.7M, +10.4%
- Operating income $465.3M vs $357.9M, +30.0%; profit $1.68 a share vs $1.27, +32.3%
- Operating ratio 70.1% vs 74.6% - costs as a share of revenue, so 29.9 cents of every dollar was kept against 25.4
- Shipments per day 42,332 vs 44,907, -5.7%; tons per day 31,804 vs 33,178, -4.1%

Now split the bill. The average shipment brought $568.55 against $485.31 a year earlier, $83.24 more. Take the fuel surcharge out and the freight itself brought $446.44 against $416.31, $30.13 more. The other $53.11 is diesel. Fuel is now $122.11 of that average bill, 21.5% of it, against $69.00 and 14.2%.

Old Dominion does not negotiate that surcharge. It moves off a weekly national diesel average the U.S. Energy Information Administration publishes every Monday: $5.599 a gallon for the week to August 31, against $3.734 a year earlier. Half as much again for the same gallon.

The profit jump underneath it is real, though. Operating expenses rose $38.9M on $146.3M more revenue, and payroll fell from 47.7% of revenue to 44.2% while less freight went through the door.

Then September 3, when Old Dominion published its August figures. Tons per day -0.9%, against -4.1% in the June quarter; shipments per day -2.4%, against -5.7%. The volume decline has nearly stopped. Same release, the other half: revenue per hundred pounds +11.3% for the quarter so far, +4.8% once fuel comes out, against +15.2% and +5.5% in June. The two halves are trading places.

Six styles, one carrier:

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - PARTIAL, and why it sits here. Wants a good business marked down after something visible and dated. Marked down is settled: Friday sits 25.3% under the $248.73 of June 9 and 17.9% under the $226.28 of July 28, the session before that quarter went out. So is the business, with no long-term debt at all against $283.9M of cash on June 30. Cheap is the half that fails. The first half earned $2.82 a share, so the price is about 33 times that pace of profit, and the discount rests entirely on those earnings holding. CHANGE IT: that 4.8%. Hold it while tonnage turns positive and the markdown was wrong.

- QUALITY-VALUE - NOT A FIT, and the closest miss. Wants a business nobody could rebuild, at a price short of its worth. Rebuilding is genuine: a freight terminal beside a big city is a zoning fight and years of one, not a purchase, and there are more than 260 of them. Price is what fails, with no markdown to lean on - 33 times the first half's pace on a shipment count down 5.7%. CHANGE IT: a full year holding an operating ratio near 70% while tonnage grows, making today's margin a level rather than a cycle peak.

- MOMENTUM - NOT A FIT. Wants a price near its twelve-month best with the recent and longer stretches of the climb agreeing. They flatly contradict: -12.1% over a month, -23.4% over three, -4.2% over six, +24.9% across twelve. CHANGE IT: a close above $248.73.

- GROWTH - NOT A FIT. Wants real expansion nobody has already paid for. Here the expansion is what is missing, not the price: profit per share rose 32.3% while the freight shrank, and six months brought 3.8% revenue growth on tonnage down 5.9%. A rate card and a fuel index are not expansion. CHANGE IT: that August -0.9% turning positive with the yield still rising.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT. Wants cash genuinely reaching owners and funded by the business. Funded is settled: six months produced $646.3M of operating cash - money kept after running the business - against $139.6M spent on trucks and terminals, and $360.4M went back to owners, $239.7M of it buybacks. As income it barely registers, at $0.29 a quarter, about 0.62% of Friday's price, next paid September 16. CHANGE IT: a payment an owner could plan around rather than round off.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT, furthest off. Wants a business early as well as fast. Fast is arguable, and it came from a price. Early is not, at a company founded in 1934. CHANGE IT: nothing realistic.

Saia at $357.94, +$12.13 / +3.51% on Friday is the same three months read the other way. The Johns Creek, Georgia company runs 218 terminals in the identical business and chose volume: its July 30 quarter grew tonnage per workday 8.4% and shipments per workday 4.4%, against Old Dominion's -4.1% and -5.7%, on revenue of $956.5M, +17.1%. It discloses the fuel share outright, 22.3% of revenue against 14.6% a year earlier, so the diesel lift belongs to the industry rather than to one company's cleverness. What Saia lacks is the margin: an operating ratio of 86.9% keeps 13.1 cents of each revenue dollar against Old Dominion's 29.9. August said it again, Saia tonnage +8.7% against Old Dominion's -0.9%. The freight exists. Old Dominion is declining to haul it at the price on offer. Saia fits none of the six Len5es, because earnings that swing with a fuel index and a volume push leave the value styles no settled base and the growth styles no record to carry forward.

Diesel is weather. It arrives, it leaves, and the bill moves with it either way. The number that is actually Old Dominion's own is what it charges to move the pallet before any of that: 5.5% higher in the June quarter, 4.8% higher since. That figure sits in the third-quarter report, undated so far, with last year's landing October 29 - and it will be printed on a network running 2,575 fewer shipments a day than a year ago. The freight comes back only at a price, and the price is the exact thing Old Dominion has spent a year protecting by letting the freight go.

Not investment advice.

Washington State 

WA State Dept. of Natural Resources (DNR)

CERTIFIED BURNER PROGRAM

Sept. 7, 2026

Forest Resilience Division 
 
Prescribed Fire Program - Certified Burner Program

The Washington State Legislature granted DNR the authority to establish a certified burner program in 2018 when it adopted House Bill 2733.

DNR launched the program in the spring of 2022 to help educate professionals and private citizens gain the knowledge and skills needed to successfully implement prescribed fire on their landscapes. 

Program Manager Kyle Lapham and recent graduate Lucas King recently participated in a webinar about the program.

The multi-day workshops happen 2-3 times each year in different parts of the state. Instruction include both classroom and field work. More information about upcoming workshops can be found below.

How to Become a Certified Prescribed Burn Manager in Washington State

The Washington State Department of Natural Resources offers three-day, in-person courses several times each year. Coursework includes four hours of prep work before the class, two days of classroom instruction, a site visit, and a final exam. Topics include fire behavior, smoke management, safety, and more. Participants must have experience leading either pile or broadcast burns. Access to property suitable for prescribed fire is required for certification.

The next step after finishing the course and passing the exam is to draft a burn plan.

Burn plans must include:

Landowner name and address
Description of the burn area
Map of the burn area
Estimated fuel tonnage per acre
Objectives of the proposed burn
Acceptable weather parameters
Summary of methods to start, control, and extinguish the burn
Neighbor notifications
Once a burn plan is completed, a prospective certified burner must obtain all necessary burn permits and authorizations from the Washington State Department of Natural Resources. Make sure to notify nearby residents and emergency response agencies about the upcoming burn. The final step is to successfully lead and implement a prescribed fire under observation by the CPBM program manager.

Burn leaders will be evaluated using this form, as well as on their burn plan and a map of the burn. Courses are held in different locations throughout Washington. There is no cost to attend; travel expenses are not covered. Interested in applying for an upcoming course? contact Program Manager Kyle Lapham.

Visit the prescribed fire page for more information about the Washington DNR Prescribed Fire Program.
